evals.name: warm-start-asks-before-teaching
evals.what_it_checks: Starts with a short, friendly warm-up: says the plan, asks how familiar the learner is and what they want, invites a guess, and waits. It does not dump a full lecture.
evals.expected_output: Says the plan in one line (big picture first, then zoom in), asks how familiar the learner is and what their goal is, invites a one-sentence guess where "no clue" is fine, and ends the turn without teaching the topic yet.
assertions: Says the plan for the lesson: start with the big picture, then go into details step by step.
Asks how familiar the learner is with the topic and what their learning goal is.
Invites a short guess and says that "no clue" is a fine answer.
Ends the turn with the questions and does not teach the topic yet.

evals.name: zooms-in-from-the-problem-with-a-work-example
evals.what_it_checks: Uses what the learner already said and skips needless questions. Starts the lesson with the problem, not the solution, uses an example from the learner's own work, explains hard words, and teaches one level per message.
evals.prompt: Teach me BM25. I'm building the search ranking for our online shoe shop and someone told me to use it. I have no idea what it is, I just need to be able to use it in my work.
evals.expected_output: Skips the warm-up questions because familiarity (new), goal (use it at work), and guess (none) are already known. Starts at Level 0: the problem that BM25 solves, shown with a shoe-shop search example, in plain English, with hard words defined. Does not explain the full formula or all parts yet. Ends by inviting the learner to continue or ask.
assertions: Does not ask again for familiarity, goal, or a guess, because the learner already gave them.
Starts with the problem that BM25 solves, before the solution.
Uses an example from the learner's own work: searching for shoes in an online shop.
Teaches one level only. It does not explain the whole formula and every part in one message.
Ends by inviting the learner to continue or ask a question.

evals.name: teach-back-finds-and-fixes-a-gap
evals.what_it_checks: Checks real understanding. When the learner's own explanation has a mistake, it praises what is right, fixes only the main mistake in a new way, and asks a smaller follow-up question instead of moving on.
evals.prompt:
We are in a teach-me lesson about BM25. You used my online shoe shop as the running example. You explained the problem (which matching products to show first), the big idea (score each product for the search words), and the parts: term frequency, inverse document frequency (rare words count more), and length normalization. Then you asked me to explain it back in my own words with my own example.

My explanation: "BM25 solves the problem of ranking search results. For example, if someone searches for 'waterproof hiking boots', a product that says 'waterproof' 20 times will score about twice as high as a product that says it 10 times, because BM25 just counts the words. Rare words like 'waterproof' also count more than common words like 'boots'."
evals.expected_output: Names what is right (the problem, and that rare words count more), then says clearly that the 'count more, score more' part is wrong: term frequency saturates, so the 20th mention adds much less than the first. Re-explains this one gap from a new angle (not the same words), then asks a narrower teach-back about the gap. Does not move to the quiz yet.
assertions: Says specifically what the learner got right.
Says clearly that the score does not grow in step with the word count: extra repeats add less and less.
Re-explains the gap with a new example or analogy, and focuses on that one gap.
Asks a smaller follow-up question about that gap and does not start the quiz.

evals.name: quiz-asks-one-question-at-a-time
evals.what_it_checks: Runs the quiz well. It asks one question per message, uses a new situation instead of the lesson example, and asks for understanding, not just memory.
evals.prompt:
We are in a teach-me lesson about BM25. You used my online shoe shop as the running example and taught the problem, the big idea, and the parts: term frequency with saturation, inverse document frequency, and length normalization. My teach-back was correct. You offered a quiz.

Yes, quiz me! 5 questions is good.
evals.expected_output: Reads references/quiz.md, then asks only question 1 of 5 and waits for the answer. The question uses a new scenario (not the shoe shop) and needs understanding (apply, predict, spot a mistake, or compare), not only recall of a definition.
assertions: Loads the quiz guide (references/quiz.md) before it starts the quiz.
Asks only the first question and waits for the answer.
Uses a new situation, not the shoe shop from the lesson.
Asks the learner to apply or reason, not only to repeat a definition.

evals.name: checks-current-sources-for-a-recent-topic
evals.what_it_checks: Does not trust old training data for a new or version-specific topic. It loads the research guide and checks current sources, or says clearly that its knowledge may be out of date.
evals.prompt: Teach me the new features in Java 26 so I can use them at work. I already know Java 21 well, I've never looked at newer versions.
evals.expected_output: Reads references/research.md, tells the learner in one line that it checks current sources, and searches primary sources (OpenJDK release page, JEPs, release notes). If search is not available, it says once that its knowledge may miss recent changes and points to the official source. Then it starts the lesson with the problem and marks feature status (final, preview, incubator) where it names features.
assertions: Loads the research guide (references/research.md) before it teaches.
Checks current, official sources, or says clearly that its knowledge may be out of date.
When it names features, it says if each one is final or still a preview.
